newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE coffee flips higher, New York chase resumes.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE coffee flips higher, New York chase resumes.

text.p: After a dip below $1,600, London robusta coffee flipped higher on Wednesday as it chased the rallying New York contracts higher.
"The market has been up and down. We are guided by New York which is volatile," said one trader.

Although London showed signs of exhaustion initially, retreating to $1,590 at one stage on trader profit taking, sentiment quickly reversed as CSCE March coffee climbed to new contract highs, touching 171.00 cents per lb after the London close.
Traders said London contracts had absorbed speculative buying on the way up while roasters had bought early on as the market weakened.
The benchmark May contract finished the session at $1,667 a tonne, a rise of $24 on the day. Its highest point was $1,685, surpassing Tuesday's near six-month high of $1,680.
"When you have so much volatility people tend to go in and out and that boosts the volume," a trader said, adding that turnover featured heavy switching activity.
London's strong close is set to boost the technical outlook further with analysts now projecting a relatively smooth rise to $1,800.
But some traders caution that the market could be open to an ambush by speculative funds which may be tempted to take profits.
"The big question is will the funds continue to buy. It may be that they are up to the limit," said one trader.
"Also I don't see the aggressive scale-up buying in London that you get in New York," he said.

The arbitrage between New York and London widened to 85 cents on May and traders said roasters could be looking to change their blend to include more robusta but the scope for such shifts could be limited.
"There is some scope for that, although it's not massive," said one.

The New York market was kept buoyant by a state-sector strike in Colombia which entered its second day. A senior official said coffee shipments to the ports had been adversely affected although he was not able to give an exact figure.
Road freight has dropped by 30 percent as fear of leftist guerrilla attacks and disruption by striking workers has kept many trucks off the roads.

Julian Parra, commercial director of the Colombian Transport Federation said traditional products such as flowers and coffee were among the most affected, but added that the situation was beginning to get back to normal.
